title: Side by side, closed

cards: Kondanna is sitting in a deer park with four old companions, listening to the man they once walked away from. The talk is still going when something comes clear for him: whatever arises also passes away.
Then, the Pali account says, a shout goes up. The earth spirits cry out that the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling, and that no one in the world can stop it.
The cry is passed up from one heaven to the next, until the whole universe shakes. The discourse is named for that moment: setting the wheel rolling.

teach.b: This block set the schools side by side, and today it closes, so walk the wheel once more. First, the hub: what all share. The four truths and the eightfold path.
The three jewels: the Buddha, the teaching, the community. Precepts, meditation, kindness.
Second, the spokes that differ. The three turnings, a Mahayana map. The arahant, honored in Theravada, and the bodhisattva, honored in the Mahayana.
One Buddha or many. Buddha-nature, inborn or grown. Emptiness and not-self.
Rebirth, taught and questioned. Lay and monastic. Devotion and meditation.
Third, the rim, where the wheel touches the road. Three canons, four languages, robes in saffron, maroon, gray and black. Festivals on different days for one birth.
Councils where the schools meet. The reason this path ranks none of them, and the door you might call home. Fourth, the picture.
Tradition reads the eight spokes of the dharma wheel as the eightfold path, which you met as eight spokes back in year two.
Spokes point in different directions and need each other to make a wheel. Take one out and it wobbles. Hold them all to the same hub and it rolls.
The cry in the deer park said no one could stop the wheel. It didn't say it would roll in only one land, one language, one color of robe.
Next, a new block: the practice traditions, the chants and sittings and walks each school does with its body.

how: Buddhists across the schools use the dharma wheel as a sign of the teaching, and some temples and centers mark the anniversary of the first teaching, recalling the wheel set rolling in the deer park.

o: a council where the schools voted on one shared creed
the schools set next to each other, none ranked above another

games.q: you're Kondanna in the deer park. the Buddha has just finished his first teaching. what happens?
o: you see that whatever arises also passes away.
you ask him to write it down first.
games.why: Kondanna sees it, and the cry goes up from the earth to the heavens: the wheel has been set rolling.

practice: On each out-breath, name one school you've met and let a little thanks go toward it: Theravada, with its forest monks and morning chants; Zen, with its silence and breakthroughs; Tibetan Buddhism, with its maroon robes and long canon; Pure Land, with its chanted name.
You don't need to agree with each one, only thank it for the people it has carried.

wordCard.voice: Side by side. The schools of Buddhism set next to each other, each taught in its own terms, none ranked: different spokes on one turning wheel. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dhammacakka (Sanskrit dharmachakra): the wheel of the teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: one wheel. Many schools, one hub. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.
